title: WWE Star Bronson Reed Dies at 38
description:
WWE star Bronson Reed died Friday at the age of 38, the WWE confirmed in a statement.

	The Australian-born wrestler, whose real name was Jermaine
body:
WWE star Bronson Reed died Friday at the age of 38, the WWE confirmed in a statement.

	The Australian-born wrestler, whose real name was Jermaine Haley, died “due to medical complications,” the league said.

	“Jermaine was a larger-than-life figure in WWE, but more importantly, he was a phenomenal person, a devoted family man and a beloved colleague. Our thoughts and deepest condolences are with Jermaine’s entire family, including his pregnant wife, Paige, their daughter, as well as all his friends, co-workers and fans,” the WWE said.
	

	Haley was raised in Adelaide and got his start working “throughout Australia’s independent scene and wrestled for a number of local promotions, including International Wrestling Australia and Melbourne City Wrestling,” according to a report by Variety Australia.

	Haley joined WWE in 2019 and made his first appearance on the league’s up-and-comers series “NXT.” He was released by WWE in 2021 but came back the following year and had remained active with the league until Friday.

	Per Variety Australia, Haley “made his way into the main event scene in 2025 as part of The Vision faction, alongside Seth Rollins, fellow prospect Bron Breakker and arguably WWE’s greatest ever talker, Paul Heyman.”

	In an interview with Rolling Stone AU/ZN last year, Haley said: “I think for me, a big change is when I got released from WWE and I came back, I sort of came back with a little bit of a chip on my shoulder, knowing that I need to be as confident as possible and show them I can do this. I’m supposed to be here,” according to Variety Australia.
	

	He recently appeared at WWE’s Crown Jewel event in Saudi Arabia.

schema.headline: WWE Star Bronson Reed Dies at 38

title: France Knights ‘Autobiography,’ ‘Tiger Stripes’ Producer Yulia Evina Bhara at JAFF Market
description: Indonesian producer Yulia Evina Bhara, whose credits include Venice title “Autobiography” and Cannes Critics’ Week winner “Tiger Stripes,” was name
body:
Indonesian producer Yulia Evina Bhara, whose credits include Venice title “Autobiography” and Cannes Critics’ Week winner “Tiger Stripes,” was named a Chevalier dans l’Ordre des Arts et des Lettres at a ceremony at JAFF Market in Yogyakarta.

	Fabien Penone, France’s ambassador to Indonesia, Timor-Leste and ASEAN, presented the insignia for France’s culture minister. The ceremony doubled as the opening of the Indonesia-France Film Lab booth at the market, which runs Nov. 25–30.
	

	France created the order in 1957, and its cinema honorees range from Agnès Varda, François Truffaut, Martin Scorsese and Isabelle Huppert to Indonesia’s Garin Nugroho. Filmmaker Joko Anwar received it last year.

	“When I read the names of the people who received this before me, I felt very small,” Bhara said. “They are writers, painters, musicians, directors, and many of them are my heroes. So when the letter came, my first thought was, maybe this is a mistake. My second was, this is not only for me, and this is true. A film producer never works alone. A producer is like a person who builds a boat, but the boat only moves when people row together.”

	In his address, Penone traced Bhara’s path from Way Kanan in Sumatra’s Lampung province through seven years of producing historical theater, a craft she taught herself, before she turned to film in 2012 with a foundation that used art to revisit the past. She set up KawanKawan Media in Jakarta in 2016, with international co-production at the core of the business from day one. The company’s name is Indonesian for “friends.”

	Its first feature, Yosep Anggi Noen’s “Solo, Solitude,” bowed at Locarno that year and later took the Golden Hanoman Award at the Jogja-Netpac Asian Film Festival. Makbul Mubarak’s “Autobiography” premiered in Venice in 2022 and went on to become Indonesia’s Oscar submission. “Tiger Stripes” won the Critics’ Week Grand Prize in 2023, and Bhara co-produced “Renoir,” which played in competition at Cannes in 2025. That same year she sat on the Critics’ Week jury.
	

	This year she co-produced Next Step Studio Indonesia, which launched as the Critics’ Week’s new talent initiative and paired four young Indonesian filmmakers with four from across Southeast Asia. The result premiered at Cannes to a standing ovation. Bhara also heads international cooperation at the Indonesian Film Board (BPI), is active in producers’ body Aprofi and has been one of the Film Lab’s driving forces since its launch.

	“Without question, you rank among the most respected producers in Indonesia,” Penone said. “Your work has helped Indonesian cinema reach new audiences and gain new recognition.”

	Bhara, who said she grew up in a small village by a forest and that her family was very poor, recalled that one of the first films she ever watched was Nugroho’s “Cinta dalam Sepotong Roti,” and that nearly every film she has produced was a multi-country effort, with partners from Singapore, Malaysia, the Philippines, Japan, Taiwan, Germany, Poland, Qatar and France.

	She told the room that independent cinema now faces three pressures, the first being big money and content, with young directors often told their stories are too small and too local. “I believe the opposite: the more local a story is, the more universal it can become,” Bhara said. “Second, attention. Fifteen seconds, then we swipe. But cinema is the art of staying. The third, the machine. AI can make images, the voices in a second, but a machine cannot remember what it feels like to lose someone.”

	The Film Lab is run by the French Embassy and Institut Français d’Indonésie together with Indonesia’s Ministry of Culture, BPI and Aprofi, backed by French film agency CNC and Paris film school La Fémis. Six Indonesian director-producer teams were picked this year, with Éric Collin, Vincent Wang, Thibault Amti and Sébastien Chesneau among the mentors. The lab continues for the next six months.

	“A first edition is an experiment. The second one is a test. A third edition tells us that something has become a habit, an institutional relationship,” said BPI chair Fauzan Zidni, whose organization joined the initiative for the first time this year. A producer who has chased international co-productions for 14 years, Zidni said he had gone to markets alone in search of partners, and pledged that BPI would keep supporting the projects after the lab ends.
	

	Penone said most projects from earlier editions will head to Paris early next month for the Southeast Asia Film Forum’s inaugural co-production meetings, staged with CNC backing and the Centre Pompidou as partner. BPI members and filmmaker Edwin will also attend.

	“Chevalier means a knight. A knight promises to protect something,” Bhara said. “So today, I promise I will keep protecting the fragile voices, the local films, the human films, and I promise I will never do it alone.”

title: How to Watch the 2026 Thanksgiving Day Parade: A Dolly Parton Tribute, Broadway Medley and Mystery Harry Potter Float
description:
If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission.

	Dolly Par
body:
If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission.

	Dolly Parton will be honored with a special musical tribute at this year’s Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade, which celebrates its historic 100th edition on Saturday after being postponed from Thanksgiving Day due to weather conditions.

	Tony-nominated Broadway star Megan Hilty will lead the tribute to the country music icon, who died in August at age 80. The performance is among several high-profile musical numbers planned for the milestone celebration, alongside appearances from RAYE, Teddy Swims, Megan Moroney, Queen Latifah and “KPop Demon Hunters” breakout EJAE.
	

	The 2026 Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade will air Saturday, Nov. 28, from 8:30 a.m. to noon in all time zones on NBC and Telemundo, with an encore presentation on NBC at 2 p.m. ET/PT. Those without cable can stream the festivities live on Peacock, in addition to a variety of live TV streaming services that carry NBC, including DirecTV, Hulu + Live TV and Sling TV in select markets.

	“Today” show personalities Savannah Guthrie, Hoda Kotb and Al Roker will return to host the Emmy-winning telecast.

	The parade’s 100th edition coincides with NBC’s own centennial anniversary, marking a particularly significant year for the network. More than 11,000 volunteers and participants will descend on Manhattan for Thursday’s festivities, which will span 2.5 miles from the Upper West Side to Macy’s flagship store in Herald Square. In a nod to the anniversary, Macy’s has assembled a record 100 inflatable creations, including new balloons depicting Bluey, Sorcerer’s Apprentice Mickey Mouse and Snoopy’s Joe Cool alter ego. The parade will also bring back balloons designed by some of the art world’s biggest names, including Tim Burton, Keith Haring, Jeff Koons and Yayoi Kusama.
	

	Hollywood will be well represented among this year’s new floats, too, including a Hogwarts-themed creation from HBO. A commemorative Macy’s All Stars float will bring together familiar characters from throughout the parade’s history, from Bugs Bunny and Scooby-Doo to Sonic the Hedgehog.

	Broadway, a fixture of the annual telecast, will get an expanded showcase this year. A 10-minute musical medley introduced by Julianne Hough will bring together performers from nine productions, including “Hamilton,” “Wicked,” “Rent,” “Chicago,” “The Book of Mormon,” “Aladdin,” “Schmigadoon!,” “The Lost Boys” and “The Rocky Horror Show.”

	Other musical performers on this year’s roster include Natasha Bedingfield, Jimmy Fallon and the Roots, Keke Palmer, JoJo, Wyclef Jean, Leslie Odom Jr., Anthony Ramos, Indigo Girls, DEVO, Smash Mouth and K-pop boy band RIIZE. The Radio City Rockettes will also return before Santa Claus closes out the festivities.

	Stream the 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade live on Peacock, or watch for free with an eligible streaming trial through DirecTV.

schema.headline: How to Watch the 2026 Thanksgiving Day Parade: A Dolly Parton Tribute, Broadway Medley and Mystery Harry Potter Float

title: Southeast Asian Cinema’s Global Rise Needs Long-Term Backing to Last, Says JAFF Chief Ifa Isfansyah
description: The quality and international profile of Southeast Asian cinema have grown sharply, and Ifa Isfansyah, festival director of Indonesia’s Jogja-Netpa
body:
The quality and international profile of Southeast Asian cinema have grown sharply, and Ifa Isfansyah, festival director of Indonesia’s Jogja-Netpac Asian Film Festival (JAFF), wants countries to build on that by treating film as part of their cultural strategy.

	He singles out the Philippines for its consistency in developing talent and keeping a presence abroad.

	“I would say that, for now, it is still more of an anomaly than a fundamental structural shift,” Isfansyah tells Variety. “However, international recognition is still largely driven by the strength of individual films and filmmakers, rather than by a broader, sustained strategy to strengthen cinema as part of a country’s cultural infrastructure.”
	

	Isfansyah is also one of Indonesia’s leading independent producers. He founded Forka Films, formerly Fourcolours Films, in 2001, and his producing credits include Kamila Andini’s “Yuni” and “Before, Now & Then,” as well as her latest, “Four Seasons in Java,” which played Toronto’s Centerpiece program and Busan this year.

	“I believe countries need to recognize cinema as an important part of their cultural strategy, not merely as an industry or a source of national prestige,” he says. “This requires long-term investment, institutional support, and a commitment to building sustainable connections with the international film community.”

	JAFF’s 21st edition drew more than 1,000 submissions, from which the festival picked 254 films from 34 countries. The program runs under the theme “Influx,” opening with Lawrence Fajardo’s Filipino drama “Silenced Nights” and closing with Ueda Makoto’s Japanese comedy-drama “You Are the Film.”
	

	Isfansyah says the current social, political and economic climate pushed the team to rethink what staging a festival should mean this year. “We did not want JAFF to become a celebration disconnected from the realities around us. This is not a moment for an excessively festive atmosphere or for pretending that everything is fine.”

	Fajardo’s film, he says, speaks directly to present-day anxieties. Opening with it was meant to signal that “cinema must remain connected to the world we live in, and a festival should not be afraid to confront difficult realities.”

	The closer is pitched partly at younger viewers, as a reminder of where JAFF came from. “JAFF began with a love for films like this, films that may not necessarily be grand in scale or production, but possess sincerity, imagination, and a strong cinematic voice,” Isfansyah says. “I think it is important to remember that a film does not have to be big to be powerful.”

	Among the submissions, he noticed filmmakers growing bolder, especially in shorts, with more of them playing with form and blurring fiction and nonfiction. “Short films are increasingly becoming spaces for creative risk-taking,” he says, rather than mere stepping stones to features.

	Many films were also more political, though not always in the sense of tackling institutions or specific events. “There is a growing urgency to tell stories that respond to the realities surrounding us.”

	The “Influx” theme also nods to change across Asian cinema, from a new generation pushing against established storytelling to shifts in how films get financed and reach audiences. “However, I think it is important to look beyond the idea of change as simply a matter of technological or industrial transformation. We should also ask where these currents are taking us, whose voices are shaping the direction of Asian cinema, and what kind of future we are building together,” Isfansyah says.

	On Indonesia’s local box office boom, he sees no hard line between the country’s commercial, arthouse, independent and genre directors. “Many filmmakers know one another, compete in a healthy way, exchange ideas, and often support each other’s work,” he says. Commercial hits, he adds, pull more people into cinemas, lift interest in local titles and draw investment, while challenging independent work keeps the industry diverse and credible.
	

	Premieres matter, but they have never been JAFF’s main yardstick. What counts is whether a film merits a slot and whether it has already had a fair shot at the festival’s audience. “If we believe a film has not yet had the opportunity to reach JAFF’s viewers, we will be interested in bringing it here, regardless of whether it has already premiered elsewhere.”

	As it enters its third decade, the festival wants to put back into the ecosystem that built it. This year it launched JAFF Kids, aimed at children and young audiences, and JAFF Awards, which honors individuals, institutions and initiatives in Indonesia and the wider region that have helped develop film culture. Earlier programs JAFF Community Forum and JAFF Market grew strong enough to become parallel events in their own right.

	However large JAFF gets, Isfansyah says it has to keep resting on emerging talent, industry professionals and academics, and keep all of them talking to one another.

	“For me, being community-driven does not mean remaining small. It means remembering that the festival exists because of the people who build it, participate in it, and give it meaning.”

schema.headline: Southeast Asian Cinema’s Global Rise Needs Long-Term Backing to Last, Says JAFF Chief Ifa Isfansyah

title: Anurag Kashyap, Ranjan Singh Back Haryana-Rooted Short ‘The Melody of Destiny’ as Executive Producers (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Indian auteur Anurag Kashyap (“Gangs of Wasseypur”) and producer Ranjan Singh have boarded “The Melody of Destiny,” a short film rooted in the nort
body:
Indian auteur Anurag Kashyap (“Gangs of Wasseypur”) and producer Ranjan Singh have boarded “The Melody of Destiny,” a short film rooted in the northern Indian state of Haryana, as presenters and executive producers, backing the film on the festival circuit.

	The short is the first film from Chaitanya Chugh, a 24-year-old self-taught director from Pehowa, Haryana. He produced it with Diya Panjwani and Aabhar S Dev.


	Saurabh Bansal plays Rajesh, who lives in Delhi, far from his wife and daughter in Haryana, and sings on the city’s streets in secret. He is saving for the day his daughter Priya (Miraya Sehgal), 10, gets married. She lives at home with her mother, Savitri (Nagmeet Arora). One evening, a conversation over dinner turns into a fight, and the family’s strained relationships come out into the open.
	

	Chugh shot the film guerrilla-style on Delhi’s streets. The idea came from two moments in his own life after the COVID-19 lockdown. In 2021, his mother told him she had given a saree from her wedding to a street performer who was collecting money for his daughter’s marriage. Months later, on the way to the mountains, Chugh saw a roadside banner offering 51 wedding items for INR 51,000 ($530), and the two memories came together.

	“Initially drawn from the stark reality of the importance of marriages in India, which is maligned by the illegal practice of dowry, it grew into an exploration of gendered roles and power, and how they shape family dynamics, especially in traditional setups. By looking into a household whose relationships are governed by abuse rooted in the problems of class and patriarchy, the film tries to present a documentation of these gruesome truths,” Chugh said.
	

	Most of the crew was female. The film also draws on Haryanvi folklore, which traditionally tells stories through metaphor in song.

	“The film really punches you hard at one point,” Kashyap said. “Chaitanya really knows the world that he has captured intimately in the film. It’s powerful, it’s sensitive and carries some really authentic performances. I hope the film travels far and wide.”

	Singh said it is rare to see a young filmmaker try to push boundaries with a first film, adding that Chugh “does that convincingly in ‘The Melody of Destiny.’ He definitely has a unique storytelling approach and an emotional outlook which is a must for this story. I saw the film through one of the producers Diya, and strongly felt it’s a film that should be taken to the world, and thus happy to onboard the film and try and do the same.”

title: Indonesian Cinema’s Next Chapter Is Reaching the World ‘Without Losing Our Cultural Identity,’ Says JAFF Market Director Linda Gozali
description:
Indonesia’s film industry has momentum at home. JAFF Market director Linda Gozali wants to help it travel.

	Gozali runs the industry market attach
body:
Indonesia’s film industry has momentum at home. JAFF Market director Linda Gozali wants to help it travel.

	Gozali runs the industry market attached to the Jogja-Netpac Asian Film Festival (JAFF), now in its third edition. The 2024 launch tested whether Indonesia needed a film market at all, and the industry’s answer was an emphatic yes. The 2025 edition opened the door to regional and international partners. This year, the market is taking stock of how well the business holds up against economic turmoil and political instability around the world, while widening the scope for credible partnerships at home and abroad.
	

	“Our next chapter is learning how to reach international audiences without losing our cultural identity,” Gozali tells Variety. “We aspire to become nationally indispensable, regionally relevant and internationally connected.”

	Local hits have yet to translate into comparable business abroad, which Gozali puts down to producers and filmmakers treating the home market as their first priority. “Indonesia has learned how to win its own audiences,” she says, adding that plenty of untapped local viewers still need to be brought in.

	Even so, Gozali says, a good share of Indonesian horror has sold across multiple territories, and independent films have been well received on the international festival circuit. She also notes that Indonesia is not alone in looking inward first, pointing to other populous countries such as China, India and Japan.

	“Any growth should not be mistaken for maturity,” she says. “JAFF Market’s responsibility is to transform that growth into sustainability.”
	

	That thinking draws on an industry report JAFF Market produced with Cinepoint. According to Gozali, it points to a basic mismatch between Indonesia’s volume of content production and appetite for investment on one side, and its limited exhibition infrastructure on the other.

	“Sustainable growth requires wider audience access, diversified distribution access, responsible production investment and stronger business intelligence,” Gozali says. “Our collaboration with Cinepoint is intended to encourage evidence-based industry decisions.”

	The market can already point to results. Projects that have met collaborators for their next steps include “Pangku” and “My Mother” from JAFF Future Project (JFP), and “Tikam Samurai,” “Bandits of Batavia,” “World Without Sleep,” “Timun Mas” and “Gloomy Sunday” from the JAFF IP Connection (JiPCon) strand. Joint ventures, memorandums of understanding and letters of intent have also emerged around “Khadam” and “Badut Gendong,” along with an agreement between JAFF Market and the Jakarta government.

	Gozali singles out “Slaughterground” as the clearest example of the market linking things up over time. Presented as an IP at JiPCon during the 2024 inaugural edition, it returns this year as a film in JAFF Future Project. “The IP met its destiny in JAFF Market,” she says.

	The deals, she argues, have created value beyond the event itself. But she sees the market’s main achievement as bringing the whole of Indonesia’s film industry under one roof for the first time.

	JAFF Market shares the regional calendar with Busan’s Asian Contents & Film Market (ACFM), Hong Kong FilMart and the Taiwan Creative Content Fest. “We are the new kids on the block so we want to work alongside the other established markets and learn and partner with them in areas that will strengthen our programs and also theirs,” Gozali says.

	Every market hopes to become a long-term international hub, she adds, but JAFF Market will take it one step at a time. Some ties are already in place. The market continues to collaborate with the Adelaide Film Festival, an institutional partnership Gozali says brings continuity, credibility and a route into established international networks. It also runs a reciprocal IP exchange with ACFM.

	To bring in international sales agents, distributors, financiers and streamers, the market relies on curated programs, business dialogues and matchmaking designed to move attendees from general discovery toward focused meetings with decision-makers. “We recognize that international participation must be driven by business opportunities, not simply invitations,” Gozali says. “The quality and relevance of international participation matter as much as the number of delegates or countries represented.”
	

	“As a producer myself, I recognize that one of our industry’s gaps (besides a shortage of stories or talent), is a shortage of sustained cross-border producer relationships,” she says of the market’s Producers Exchange strand, which aims to build trust, encourage knowledge sharing and help producers find compatible partners beyond one-off projects. “Connecting the right producers today can shape the regional production and distribution landscape of tomorrow.”

	For newcomers, JAFF Future Project, Film Labs and Talent Day offer a way into the Indonesian industry. Gozali says the insights gathered across the market’s programs help first-time filmmakers find their way and have shaped how they handle business with international partners.

	International co-productions open up additional financing, creative expertise, shared resources, distribution networks and new audiences. Indonesia, however, would benefit from clearer regulatory frameworks, production incentives and tax rebate mechanisms. “It is important to ensure that Indonesian filmmakers are ready to become equal creative and business partners,” Gozali says.

	JAFF Market is backed by Amar Bank, Indonesia’s Ministry of Culture and Ministry of Creative Economy, Jakarta City and a roster of sponsors and partners. Gozali is grateful for that backing but says the platform needs long-term, sustained support in both funding and infrastructure to keep serving the industry.

	“JAFF Market must remain commercially responsible without becoming commercially exclusive,” she says. Diversified revenue streams, strategic partnerships and curated programs are meant to keep the market open to independent filmmakers and emerging production companies. “Supporting emerging talent is not simply a philanthropic endeavor; it is an investment in the industry’s future creative and commercial potential,” she adds.

	As for the next five years, “Growth is not necessarily about becoming bigger,” Gozali says. “It is about becoming more relevant, useful and consequential.”

title: JAFF Market Opens Third Edition With Call to Measure Indonesian Cinema’s Growth by Quality, Not Just Volume
description: JAFF Market, which organizers bill as Indonesia’s biggest film market, opened its third edition at the Jogja Expo Center in Yogyakarta with market
body:
JAFF Market, which organizers bill as Indonesia’s biggest film market, opened its third edition at the Jogja Expo Center in Yogyakarta with market director Linda Gozali urging the local industry to judge its growth on quality as well as scale.

	The three-day market runs alongside the Jogja-Netpac Asian Film Festival (JAFF). Gozali said the first edition was conceived as an experiment. “It is actually a question that we threw into the Indonesian ecosystem whether or not we truly need a film market. And the response was definitely overwhelming,” she said.
	

	Gozali said the market’s third outing called for some reflection on whether the industry can “actually endure and survive the economic upheaval, the socio-political instability, as well as whatever issues that are actually evolving in the global era.”

	The 2025 edition centered on local and international collaboration, she said, with the goal of turning leads into multiple deals.  

	“This is a transitional period, and therefore let’s define what growth is,” Gozali added. “We have to define growth not just in terms of the quantity, no. Because growth in quantity itself will reduce at a time where there are challenges around the environment. So we look at growth as well from the quality point of view.”

	The exhibition floor hosts 116 exhibitors, and the opening day was reserved as a business day for accredited badge holders. Amar Bank is powering the market for the second year running.

	The JAFF Future Project selection comprises 12 projects. Indonesian titles are Dhiwangkara Seta’s “Absence” (stylized “αLPα”), Timoteus Anggawan Kusno’s “Orphaned Atlas” (an Indonesia-France-Netherlands co-production), “Pupus: The Orchid of Merapi,” “A Quiet Sunshine,” “Somewhere Between” and Sidharta Tata’s “Slaughterground,” along with “Gokil,” presented with Jakarta Film Week. From elsewhere come Glenn Barit’s “Luz and Flor” (Philippines), Rein Maychaelson’s “Primal” (Indonesia, Singapore, South Korea), M. Raihan Halim’s “The Smuggler” (Singapore), Boo Junfeng’s multi-country co-production “Trinity” and Rosie Lourde’s “Wreck and Ruin” (Australia), which arrives via a partnership with the Adelaide Film Festival and Malaysia’s mylab.
	

	The IP Connection strand, formerly known as JAFF Content Market, has opened to international properties for the first time. Of its 10 selections, four come from overseas: the comic “Disposable Dolly” (Hong Kong), the book “Cat Rental Company” (Taiwan) and two South Korean titles brought in through a partnership with Busan’s Asian Contents & Film Market (ACFM), the book “My Upstairs Neighbors” and the webtoon “Friend Request.” The six Indonesian properties are animation “Komarong,” board game “Mantra,” comics “Blood Upon the Snow,” “Lao Sam 1892” and “Yuuko’s Gloomy Days,” and novel “Hati-Hati Ada Dua Hati” (roughly, “Watch Out, There Are Two Hearts”).

	Among the new initiatives is a Producers Exchange, whose first batch numbers 14 producers: Lisa Scott and Rae Choi (Australia), who come via the Adelaide Film Festival, Jason Karman (Canada, Indonesia), Nana Riskhi and Nick Musa (Indonesia), Wong Kew Soon (Malaysia), Otgontuya Zorig (Mongolia), Danzen Santos Katanyag (Philippines), Sam Chua Weishi and Wendy Lie (Singapore), Kimbo Kim (South Korea), Shao-Yi Chen (Taiwan), Phimphloi Nan Saensuk (Thailand) and Rajib Mohajan (Bangladesh, U.S.). Chua is pulling double duty: she is also one of the producers of “Primal.”

	The Indonesia-France Film Lab X MTN Lab, now in its third year, is run by the French Embassy and the Institut français d’Indonésie (IFI), with Paris film school La Fémis supplying the mentors. Indonesian partners include the Ministry of Culture’s Directorate of Film, Music and Arts, whose national talent management program MTN gives the lab its name, along with the Indonesia Film Agency (BPI) and the Association of Indonesian Film Producers (Aprofi). This year’s six projects, all debut or sophomore features from director-producer pairings, are “A Straight Way to Love,” “An Interesting Incident,” “Father Figure,” “My Tears, a Sea for Jakarta to Sink,” “Saltstorm!” and “Super Neli.”

	A second new program focuses on film writing across journalism, criticism and the essay form. It has 15 young participants, among them journalists, writers, lecturers, researchers and communications professionals.

	The first day’s conference program includes a big-ideas session on where Indonesian cinema goes next, along with a session on how cultural phenomena can grow beyond trends and open doors to cross-border projects. The second day will turn to the question of where the country’s audience actually sits, with Gozali noting that many foreign collaborators arrive drawn by the “lucrative Indonesian market.” Sessions that day will also cover AI in microdramas, documentaries, budgets and what it takes for an Indonesian production house to last 30 years.
	

	“Economically speaking, we are actually in a cautious mood,” Gozali said.

	The final day will take in animation, box office breakouts and actors who have moved into producing, plus a talk on action and stunts from Japanese action director Tanigaki Kenji.

	Ahmad Mahendra, director general of culture development, utilization and fostering at Indonesia’s Ministry of Culture, delivered a brief keynote in which he said he hoped the market would keep growing and strengthening the country’s film ecosystem, and that the ministry could lend its support. The market was then declared open as guests inserted memory sticks into a projector.

	Joining Mahendra on stage were JAFF founder Garin Nugroho, festival director Ifa Isfansyah, JAFF Market executive director Ajish Dibyo, business director Sekarini Seruni, business strategist FX Iwan, board members Lorna Tee and Yulia Evina Bhara, and Amar Bank senior VP Josua Sloane. French ambassador to Indonesia Fabien Penone also attended, along with Cecep Rukendi, deputy for media creativity at the Ministry of Creative Economy, and Andhika Permata, head of Jakarta’s Tourism and Creative Economy Agency.

	“People say the third is the charm,” Gozali said. “Hopefully it is, fingers crossed.”

title: Jason Iskandar’s ‘First Breath After Coma’ Revisits Lunar New Year’s Public Return to Indonesia After a Three-Decade Ban, First Looks Unveiled (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Indonesian filmmaker Jason Iskandar‘s “First Breath After Coma,” a drama set as the country’s Chinese community prepared to celebrate the Lunar New
body:
Indonesian filmmaker Jason Iskandar‘s “First Breath After Coma,” a drama set as the country’s Chinese community prepared to celebrate the Lunar New Year openly for the first time in more than 30 years, has revealed first-look images of its three leads.

	The stills were unveiled at Indonesia’s JAFF Market, which takes place alongside the 21st Jogja-Netpac Asian Film Festival (JAFF) in Yogyakarta. They show Ladya Cheryl, Morgan Oey and Abby Latip as three siblings who find their way back to one another in Jakarta at the turn of the millennium.
	

	Written and directed by Iskandar and produced by Florence Giovani for Jakarta outfit Studio Antelope, the film follows a Chinese-Indonesian family during a period of national transition, in the days before Chinese New Year in 2000. That holiday was the first to be marked after the government formally dropped the curbs on public displays of Chinese culture.

	From 1967 to 1998, Indonesia tightly limited how Chinese culture could be expressed in public. The New Year festivities, the Chinese language and other customs survived largely behind closed doors, kept alive within families. By 2000, those traditions were starting to resurface.

	“When the restrictions were lifted, their effects did not simply disappear. They remained in everyday life, in ways that I feel are often overlooked. That is why I wanted to approach this history through a family. Through the relationships between these three siblings, we can see how our personal lives are intertwined with a much larger history. As a Chinese Indonesian, I feel that even the most personal things are already political,” said Iskandar.
	

	In one image, Cheryl grips a microphone at home, apparently in the middle of a karaoke session, a favorite pastime among Chinese Indonesians. 



	

					“First Breath After Coma”
									Tri Ranta
	



	Oey sports period glasses and hair, with a car of the era visible behind him. 



	

					“First Breath After Coma”
									Tri Ranta
	



	Latip wears a red cheongsam and stands among New Year lanterns, though her face suggests unease.

	Cheryl won the best actress Citra Award at the 2022 Indonesian Film Festival (FFI) for “Vengeance Is Mine, All Others Pay Cash,” which also won the Golden Leopard at Locarno. Oey starred in “Ghost in the Cell,” which world premiered in the Berlinale’s Forum strand this year. The film marks the feature debut of Latip, who appeared in the short “The Rootless Bloom,” a competition title at the 28th Busan International Film Festival in 2023.

	The project has been a long time coming. It began at the SGIFF Southeast Asian Film Lab in Singapore in 2015 and later went through EAVE Ties That Bind (2023/2024) in Taiwan and Italy. It was pitched at the Golden Horse Film Project Promotion (FPP) in 2024 and at the Hong Kong-Asia Film Financing Forum (HAF) in 2025.

	Giovani, Iskandar’s filmmaking partner since their early shorts, said the pair spent more than a decade developing the film. “As a Chinese Indonesian, I saw parts of my own life in this family’s story, and that personal connection is a big part of why I wanted to help Jason bring his vision to the screen. The bond between the siblings and the pull of home are things I think audiences will recognize wherever they’re from. Over the years, we found collaborators in Indonesia and across the region who connected with the story in their own ways and helped us make the film,” she said.

	Those collaborators include Singaporean cinematographer Teck Siang Lim (“Ah Girl,” “Crocodile Tears,” “Whether the Weather Is Fine”) and production designer Dita Gambiro (“Four Seasons in Java,” “Sore: A Wife From the Future,” “Cigarette Girl”). To recreate the period, the team hunted for Jakarta locations that still look much as they did in the late 1990s, and found that some corners of the city have barely changed.

	Co-producers are Yulia Evina Bhara of KawanKawan Media, Wanyi Pratiknyo and Hannan Cinthya of Arungi Films. Bhara’s “Autobiography” debuted in Venice’s Horizons section in 2022, and she co-produced “Tiger Stripes,” winner of the Cannes Critics’ Week Grand Prize in 2023. Pratiknyo co-produced “Levitating,” which played in Sundance’s World Cinema Dramatic Competition this year, while Cinthya was a co-producer on Next Step Studio Indonesia, a four-short program that screened at Cannes Critics’ Week this year.
	

	The film is in post-production and aiming for a festival premiere in 2027, to be followed by theatrical releases in Indonesia and select international territories. The film’s local title is “Perayaan Pertama.”

	“First Breath After Coma” follows Iskandar’s 2021 debut feature “Akhirat: A Love Story,” a romantic fantasy made by Studio Antelope with Base Entertainment and Ivanhoe Pictures. It opened in Indonesian theaters that December. Iskandar and Giovani founded Studio Antelope in 2011. The company has since moved into series, including “CinLock: Love, Camera, Action” for Vision+ and Netflix, and in October released Fajar Nugros’ “Bapak Paling Jujur” in local cinemas.

	Yogyakarta is familiar ground for the director. His short “Territorial Pissings” was named best short film at JAFF in 2010.

title: ‘Outlander: Blood of My Blood’ Bosses on the Season 2 Finale Twist That Would Rewrite the Series’ Lore, Who Won’t Appear on the Show — and Its Uncertain Future
description: SPOILER ALERT: This post contains spoilers from “Twelfth Night,” the Season 2 finale of “Outlander: Blood of My Blood,” now streaming on Starz.
body:
SPOILER ALERT: This post contains spoilers from “Twelfth Night,” the Season 2 finale of “Outlander: Blood of My Blood,” now streaming on Starz.

	“Outlander” was never a series to hold back on a brainy twist that took a minute to digest. But its prequel series, “Outlander: Blood of My Blood,” may have outdone its predecessor with a twist that rewrites at least one family tree.

	Since the prequel premiered last year, it has always operated on its own narrative timeline, separate from author Diana Gabaldon’s book series. In those books, Julia (Hermoine Corfield) and Henry (Jeremy Irvine), the parents of original series heroine Claire (Caitriona Balfe), died when she was 5 years old in a car crash. But with “Blood of My Blood,” executive producers Matthew B. Roberts and Maril Davis ponder what might have happened if they actually time-traveled through the same magic stones their daughter would decades later, and were left to survive in 1710s Scotland.


	It has been one tragedy after another for the lovebirds, and that’s saying something, given that they weathered World War I. But one question has loomed large over the Beauchamps: What will happen to their son, William, with whom Julia was pregnant when they went through the stones? He’s not in Gabaldon’s books, so Roberts and Davis have a bit of freedom to play with his fate. And they seemingly gave fans their answer in the Season 2 finale.



	

									Courtesy of Robert Wilson/Starz
	



	Julia and Henry were dealt their biggest setback yet earlier this season, when a seer informed her she isn’t a time traveler, she was just pregnant with one. William has his father’s mystical gene, and now that Julia is postpartum, she won’t be able to go back to her own time unless they get pregnant again, which itself is a moral quandary. The news doesn’t stop them from trying to run away together again. But in the process, Henry is shot by Lord Lovat (Tony Curran) in a case of mistaken identity, and Julia’s attempts to flee Lovat’s henchman leave her lifeless at the bottom of a waterfall. Fearful for wee William’s life without his parents, Julia’s confidante Davina (Sarah Vickers) takes him to the safest place she can think of –– to her son Brian (Jamie Roy) and his new wife Ellen (Harriet Slater). Mere moments after Brian and Ellen’s long-awaited wedding, the Frasers have a new addition to their future home at Lallybroch.


	This is where the series goes for broke, and makes a frankly brazen claim. Brian and Ellen are, of course, the parents of future “Outlander” hero Jamie (Sam Heughan). According to Gabaldon’s original books, he had an older brother named William (aka Willie), whose death when Jamie was young forever affected how he saw the world and cared for those he loved. (Not for nothing, Willie was so formative for Jamie that fans latched onto the wooden snake he carved before he died, and the onscreen prop sold for more than $5,000 at auction earlier this year.)

	If “Blood of My Blood” is to be believed, Brian and Ellen being given an infant named William could mean that Claire’s heretofore unknown younger brother was actually raised as a Fraser 200 years in the past. It’s a twist that completely alters how fans should look –– at least in the TV series’ timeline –– at Claire and Jamie’s relationship. Not only does the prequel depict their parents as unexpected allies, but it is now suggesting they may have even shared a sibling, not by blood thankfully.
	

	Now before anyone gets too excited (or angry!), Roberts and Davis aren’t exactly making this twist official on a birth certificate just yet: Even when pressed multiple times for confirmation, they dodged answering whether this really is the Willie of the Fraser family tree. But with Season 2 coming to a close without news about a Season 3 renewal, it’s hard not to feel the impact of this twist, given it could be the revelation the prequel leaves fans as a parting gift. For now, Davis is tying it all back to the original.



	

									Courtesy of Robert Wilson/Starz
	



	“With Willie/William, even if they’re not the same person, I think it’s so interesting to think how these two stories are interwoven now,” she tells Variety. “It binds Jamie and Claire’s parents, and how will that affect them in the future? We always loved the idea that Jamie and Claire were meant to be, and we’re seeing how that fate all comes together.”
	

	Roberts has a bit more fun with his response about the mystery of it all. “I feel like this is the natural place to go, and I like to manipulate people,” he says with a grin. “That’s my job.”

	He isn’t kidding. Alternate endings were filmed for the finale, one where Ellen reveals to Brian that she is pregnant again right before they are handed William (an emotional beat, given that his father caused her miscarriage this season). So this could have been a case of two Williams. But Roberts suggests it was less of a possibility, and more of a security measure.

	“I like to do some alt endings to throw people off in case scripts get leaked,” he says. “I like to keep actors on their toes, too. I have something in my head that I want to put on screen, but we did multiple endings with the finale of ‘Outlander’ as well.”

	But rewriting lore to this degree is risky business, especially given the series isn’t yet guaranteed to come back. Still, Roberts and Davis have already planned out what would happen next should they get the go ahead, and there is one thing audiences won’t ever see in this prequel: young Jamie.



	

									Courtesy of Robert Wilson/Starz
	



	While diehard fans have undoubtedly done the math to figure out just how soon their favorite Highlander could make his debut, Roberts says he is hesitant to bring the action too close to the stories told in Gabaldon’s books and the original series.

	“It’s hard to think about the stories with young Jamie in them, because that feels like you’re starting to tread on ‘Outlander,’ and I don’t want to do that,” he says. “It feels like you want to get maybe as close to the birth of Jamie as we can, but that still gives us quite a bit of time.”
	

	If “Blood of My Blood” is at least in step with Gabaldon’s book series’ timeline, Willie is born in 1716 –– the same year of Brian and Ellen’s wedding, as seen in the Season 2 finale. Jamie will be born in 1721, so five years could be what’s left of the narrative runway for the series.



	

									Courtesy of Robert Wilson/Starz
	



	With those parameters in place, Roberts and Davis also continue to look beyond “Blood of My Blood” for future “Outlander” franchise opportunities. Even with the wealth of Gabaldon’s world building at their disposal (her 10th and final book has yet to be released), they continue to be vocal about a particular contender.

	Lord John, a fan-favorite character played by David Berry in the original series, is the subject of Gabaldon’s companion series of novels, and Roberts and Davis previously tried to spin off those stories while the original “Outlander” was still airing. The series didn’t move forward then, but they seem to be actively hoping the franchise’s continued success will reignite interest.

	“There are certainly other things out there for us to explore, and Lord John remains one of them,” Davis says.

schema.headline: ‘Outlander: Blood of My Blood’ Bosses on the Season 2 Finale Twist That Would Rewrite the Series’ Lore, Who Won’t Appear on the Show — and Its Uncertain Future

title: Netflix’s ‘Secrets’ Takes Indonesian Auteur Ravi Bharwani Into Thriller Territory After Eight-Year Gap
description: Indonesian filmmaker Ravi Bharwani‘s Netflix thriller “Secrets,” his first feature in eight years, will world premiere at the 21st Jogja-Netpac Asi
body:
Indonesian filmmaker Ravi Bharwani‘s Netflix thriller “Secrets,” his first feature in eight years, will world premiere at the 21st Jogja-Netpac Asian Film Festival on Nov. 29, four days before it begins streaming on the platform on Dec. 3.

	Sha Ine Febriyanti (“This Earth of Mankind”) plays Parni, a former sex worker who now runs a beauty salon while raising her daughter on her own. Her hard-won stability is upended when Jamal (Abimana Aryasatya, “Gundala”), the violent man she once escaped, gets out of prison and comes back determined to reclaim her. Shenina Cinnamon plays Parni’s daughter Riska, and Ruth Marini plays Darsi.
	

	The film is adapted from Dewi Kharisma Michellia’s short story “Rahasia dari Kramat Tunggak” (“Secrets from Kramat Tunggak”). Its early section unfolds in 1980s Jakarta, in a milieu drawn from the Kramat Tunggak district, before the story leaps ahead to the 2000s and Jamal’s return. Bharwani co-wrote the screenplay with Rayya Makarim, who has worked with him for over a quarter century, and Wilza Lubis produced through Buddy Buddy Pictures. Both were also on board for his previous feature, 2018’s “27 Steps of May.”

	Bharwani, whose earlier features are “Impian Kemarau” (2004) and “Fishing Platform” (2008), tells Variety he spent the intervening years writing scripts and synopses, completing a couple of screenplays along the way. “But then my biggest problem is still funding, distribution, so that’s my biggest challenge,” he says. “And simply, this is the one that got financed, so I jumped in without having to wait for another few years anymore.”
	

	He was first drawn to the short story by a scene in which a woman is won in a game of chess. “I can feel the mood of the scene, the setting, the color, and the stickiness, the humidity of that scene,” Bharwani says.

	“Secrets” is his first thriller, and with it come erotic scenes, violence and action, none of which he had filmed before. He says exploring the darker side of human psychology, tackling domestic violence and working at the scale of a Netflix production made the shift difficult. That difficulty was also what drew him in.

	“For me, it’s not just about the bombastic scenes or the sensationalism,” he says. “For me, it’s how to make the audience invest in the fear, in the anger, in the hate, in being a victim, being in power of this character.”

	Bharwani set the opening in the 1980s because brothels in Kramat Tunggak operated legally then. The district was later shut down, though he notes the trade simply moved underground, and the area no longer exists. His research drew on a book about Kramat Tunggak and on Michael Glawogger’s 2011 documentary “Whores’ Glory,” which follows sex workers in several countries.

	“And then I do not try to be consistent, to be true to the setting of the 1980s, but what is important for the film, and that’s the one that I go along with,” Bharwani says. He worked closely with cinematographer Arief Retno Pribadi on color, costume and lighting so that each scene’s look matched its emotional register.

	Shaping Jamal meant ongoing conversations with Aryasatya through prep, the shoot and post-production. Bharwani says the actor has an uncle he recognized as a near-exact match for the character and grew up in a tough environment steeped in machismo, yet brings a real sensitivity to emotion and to women.

	“There are moments that we see this is too human that we see, ‘Okay, the audience will get into giving more sympathy for Jamal,'” Bharwani says. “So we need to edit it out, but at the same time not wanting to make him a one-dimensional character.”

	Indonesia is one of Asia’s largest and fastest-growing theatrical markets, but much of that growth has come from horror and other genre fare. Bharwani says his previous work relied on international festival funding that took years to secure, and the films sometimes ended up playing only at festivals.
	

	“So hopefully with Netflix over here, they spearhead the whole industry, change the whole industry setting of not just going to safe areas, going to horror, going to drama, or going to easier comedy films,” he says.

	At JAFF, “Secrets” plays in the Indonesian Screen Awards section. Editor Harin Paesongthai, production designer Menfo Tantono and composers Aghi Narottama and Tony Merle round out the key crew. Beyond promoting the film, Bharwani plans to work through the festival lineup and meet other filmmakers.

	He already has projects in the writing stage. “Making a film for me is a great chance to be able to express what I feel about humans, about environment, about stuff that I experience myself,” he says.

	By his count, he has enough material ready for two or three more films – if someone is willing to make them.
